article_title: To what extent can think sheets with or without reflection prompts support self-regulated learning from text?
citation: Anja Prinz-Weiß & Elisa Röhm. (2025). To what extent can think sheets with or without reflection prompts support self-regulated learning from text? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09419-z
title: Knowledge Revision Components (KReC) framework as the theoretical account for why think sheets address misconceptions
description: The article invokes the KReC framework (Kendeou & O'Brien, 2014) as the explanatory model for how think sheets foster conceptual change. It proposes that knowledge revision requires that "the misconception and correct information are simultaneously activated in a learner's memory (coactivation principle)", after which correct information is integrated and increasingly dominates the knowledge network (competing activation principle). Because think sheets require learners to extract correct information from a text and set it against the respective misconceptions, the authors argue they likely evoke coactivation and additional conceptual-change processes, and their generative character may additionally support transfer.
requirements: Learning materials must present both the misconception and the correct information so both can be coactivated in memory.
constraints: The framework is used interpretively; the article states the two methods "might have facilitated coactivation", not that coactivation was measured.
target_learners: University students with prior misconceptions about learning content
target_learning_goals: Revising misconceptions and building accurate conceptual understanding from texts
examples: The think sheet asked learners to answer central covariance questions with correct information from the text after reading a stated misconception for each question.
key_sources: Anja Prinz-Weiß & Elisa Röhm. (2025). To what extent can think sheets with or without reflection prompts support self-regulated learning from text? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09419-z

citation: Karel Kreijns, Kate Xu, Joshua Weidlich. (2022). Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09623-8
title: Social Presence Measure (Kreijns et al., 2020): a Rasch-validated 27-item two-dimensional measure of perceived 'realness'
description: The review presents the Social Presence Measure of Kreijns et al. (2020) as an instrument that 'operationalizes "realness" of the other persons in the communication in accordance with the reformulated social presence definition'. Rasch analyses were performed to establish construct validity; aiming at a unidimensional measure, the multidimensionality test instead revealed two dimensions, 'awareness of others' (15 items) and 'proximity with others' (12 items), with the former indicating lower and the latter higher perceptions of social presence. It uses five-point Likert scales and requires a conversion table to convert total scores to Rasch person measures.
requirements: A conversion table is needed to convert total scores to Rasch person measures
constraints: The Rasch test for multidimensionality revealed two dimensions rather than the intended unidimensional structure
target_learning_goals: assessing perceived 'realness' of communication partners in online learning
examples: Validation was by Rasch analysis with Cronbach α of 0.92 and 0.94 for the two dimensions (n = 82)
key_sources: Karel Kreijns, Kate Xu, Joshua Weidlich. (2022). Social Presence: Conceptualization and Measurement. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-021-09623-8

article_title: Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change
citation: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9
title: Knowledge Revision Components (KReC) framework of conceptual change
description: The article adopts the Knowledge Revision Components Framework by Kendeou and O'Brien (2014), which it says "is supported by strong evidence in the subject of reducing misconceptions". According to the framework, "conceptual change occurs through (1) co-activation of the misconception and the correct information that is aimed to refute the misconception", followed by (2) integration of the correct information into the relevant cognitive schema, and (3) competing-activation, in which the correct information is activated iteratively more strongly than the misconception, which is inhibited in relevant situations. Refutation texts are presented as a way to achieve co-activation.
requirements: Conceptual change requires deliberate processing, which requires active mental effort and motivation to engage with the presented information
target_learning_goals: conceptual change about scientifically unsupported beliefs
examples: The study's refutation texts name a common math-gender misconception, state that it is incorrect, and provide the correct alternative explanation to achieve co-activation
key_sources: Anna-Sophia Dersch · Ian Thacker · Alexander Eitel (2026). Should we Tell Teachers That They Are (In)Correct? How Personalized Refutation Text Promotes or Hampers Conceptual Change. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-026-10116-9

article_title: Development and Validation of a Theory-Based Questionnaire to Measure Different Types of Cognitive Load
citation: Krieglstein, F., Beege, M., Rey, G. D., Sanchez-Stockhammer, C., & Schneider, S. (2023). Development and Validation of a Theory-Based Questionnaire to Measure Different Types of Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09738-0
title: A 15-item theory-based questionnaire measuring intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load separately
description: The instrument measures the three cognitive load types separately with multiple items on a 9-point Likert-type scale, developed from a 17-item catalog and reduced to 15 items (five per type). Items intended to measure ICL and ECL "were formulated passively", while "the items designed to measure GCL were formulated from a first-person perspective (“I”)" to make the active investment of cognitive resources easier to assess. The strict use of "learning content" (ICL) versus "design or structure of the learning material" (ECL) wording was chosen because learners have problems differentiating ICL from ECL, and one ICL item explicitly addresses prior knowledge.
requirements: Appropriate instruction is needed so respondents assess the learning intervention rather than a subsequent learning test.
constraints: The article states the construct germane cognitive load remains controversial concerning its measurement and theoretical embedding in cognitive load theory.
target_learning_goals: differentiated measurement of perceived intrinsic, extraneous, and germane cognitive load during learning
examples: Studies 3–5 were designed so that "each cognitive load type was manipulated separately (Study 3: ICL; Study 4: ECL; Study 5: GCL) to further validate the questionnaire" in between-subjects online experiments.
key_sources: Krieglstein, F., Beege, M., Rey, G. D., Sanchez-Stockhammer, C., & Schneider, S. (2023). Development and Validation of a Theory-Based Questionnaire to Measure Different Types of Cognitive Load. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-023-09738-0

article_title: Evaluating the Effects of Mother Tongue on Math and Science Instruction
citation: Behrmann, T. (2018). Evaluating the effects of mother tongue on math and science instruction. Monument, CO, USA: ISTES Organization. https://www.istes.org
title: Kreyol-medium math and science intervention with a nonequivalent control group pre-test/post-test design and switching replication
description: The intervention taught the same math and science concepts to two groups of Haitian students, one in Kreyol and one in French, with the researcher as sole instructor. The article states: "This study was a quasi -experimental research, which used the nonequivalent control group design with pre -test and post -test for an experimental an d control group." Students completed pre-tests before and post-tests after instruction, and a student perception questionnaire on learning in each language. The target population was 246 girls at a private school in Haiti, sampled by consecutive sampling.
requirements: Groups formed by consecutive sampling with a switching replication method so French-condition participants also experience the Kreyol condition in consecutive interventions
constraints: The study was conducted at an all-female school, which the author states limits generalization to both genders
The academic schedule and state exams constrained timing, and the study ran over a short period
target_learners: Secondary girls at a private Haitian school (246 students across grade levels)
target_learning_goals: Student perceptions of language of instruction and Haitian identity
examples: The researcher taught the same concept to the French condition group in French and the Kreyol condition group in Kreyol, with pre-tests before and post-tests after instruction, analyzed via repeated measures ANCOVA
key_sources: Behrmann, T. (2018). Evaluating the effects of mother tongue on math and science instruction. Monument, CO, USA: ISTES Organization. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED603513

article_title: Evaluating the Effects of Mother Tongue on Math and Science Instruction
citation: Behrmann, T. (2018). Evaluating the effects of mother tongue on math and science instruction. I. Sahin & T. Shelley (Eds.). Monument, CO, USA: ISTES Organization. https://www.istes.org
title: Kreyol-medium math and science intervention with nonequivalent control group design and switch replication
description: The study's intervention taught the same math and science concepts to two student groups, one in Kreyol and one in French, at an all-female private school in Haiti with 246 girls in the target population. It used a quasi-experimental nonequivalent control group design with pre-test and post-test, consecutive non-random sampling, and a switching replication method in which French-condition participants also experienced the Kreyol condition in consecutive interventions. Data included achievement tests, a student perception questionnaire, and group interviews.
requirements: Pre-tests to assess prior knowledge before instruction and post-tests after instruction in each condition
constraints: Conducted at an all-female school, limiting generalization to male students; constrained by the academic schedule of standardized state exams and by a short study duration
target_learners: Haitian secondary girls at Institution X
target_learning_goals: Math and science concept acquisition in the language of instruction
examples: The researcher taught the same concept to the French condition group in French and the Kreyol condition group in Kreyol, collecting pre- and post-test data from both
key_sources: Behrmann, T. (2018). Evaluating the effects of mother tongue on math and science instruction. I. Sahin & T. Shelley (Eds.). Monument, CO, USA: ISTES Organization. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED623098

article_title: Fostering Early Numerical Skills at School Start in Children at Risk for Mathematical Achievement Problems: A Small Sample Size Training Study
citation: Marcus Hasselhorn & Kathrin Linke-Hasselhorn. (2013). Fostering Early Numerical Skills at School Start in Children at Risk for Mathematical Achievement Problems: A Small Sample Size Training Study. International Education Studies, 6(3). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/ies.v6n3p213
title: Krajewski's developmental model of quantity-number competence levels (I-III)
description: The article describes a three-level developmental model of early number competence. At Level I children distinguish "the scopes and extents of quantities" and rehearse number words without linking them to quantities. At Level II number words become linked to quantities, first imprecisely (IIa, rough categories like "many") and then precisely (IIb, allocating counted quantities to the exact order of numbers). At Level III children understand relations between numbers, decomposing numbers and expressing quantity differences with numbers. The article uses this model to structure the MZZ program's three intervention priorities and to define the precursor skills targeted for at-risk children.
requirements: The model assumes basic numerical skills such as counting and quantity differentiation are linked at approximately kindergarten age before precise quantity-to-number-word linkage can develop
constraints: The article states Level III integrates understanding of calculating operations and is generally only acquired for certain in the first school year, so the first two levels are the precursory competencies
target_learners: school-entry children with weak mathematical precursor skills
examples: The MZZ program's three focal areas map onto the levels: basic skills (Level I), precise quantity-number-word linkage (IIb), and number relations (Level III)
key_sources: Marcus Hasselhorn & Kathrin Linke-Hasselhorn. (2013). Fostering Early Numerical Skills at School Start in Children at Risk for Mathematical Achievement Problems: A Small Sample Size Training Study. International Education Studies, 6(3). http://dx.doi.org/10.5539/ies.v6n3p213
